property_summary: Only the owner can successfully call withdrawAll (calls to withdrawAll revert for non-owners).
Calls to withdrawAll revert for callers who are not the contract owner.
Calling withdrawAll succeeds iff the caller is the owner (so non-owners' calls revert).
Only the owner can successfully call withdrawAll (calls to withdrawAll revert for non-owners).

In the reference contract only the owner can cause the contract to send Ether via sendMoney/withdrawAll; the mutant inverts onlyOwner allowing non-owners to trigger outgoing transfers which can change the contract balance when non-owner calls happen, so the rule is that after a non-owner invokes sendMoney forwarding some value, the contract balance remains unchanged in the reference but can change in the mutant for some inputs.

For any caller and any value, when a non-owner calls sendMoney(target, value) forwarding value from the contract, the reference contract preserves its balance (no Ether leaves the contract), whereas the mutant (which inverts onlyOwner) can let a non-owner trigger outgoing transfers and thus reduce the contract balance for some inputs.

For every caller address and value, calling sendMoney(target, value) does not change the contract balance when the caller is not the owner (reference enforces onlyOwner so non-owners cannot trigger outgoing transfers), whereas the mutant inverts onlyOwner allowing some non-owner calls to cause outgoing transfers and reduce address(c).balance for some inputs.

For every non-owner caller and any positive value, calling sendMoney(target, value) on the correct contract never changes address(c).balance (call is disallowed by onlyOwner), while the mutant inverts the check so some non-owner calls succeed and can reduce address(c).balance.

For every caller and amount, if a non-owner attempts to invoke sendMoney on the correct contract the call is rejected (so address(c).balance does not decrease), whereas the mutant that inverts onlyOwner allows some non-owners to call sendMoney and thereby can reduce address(c).balance for some inputs.

For any caller who is the owner and for any positive contract balance, calling withdrawAll transfers the contract's entire balance out (reducing address(c).balance to zero); the mutant removed the internal call so withdrawAll does not withdraw the balance and thus can leave a non-zero contract balance.

For any nonzero deposit amount and when the owner calls withdrawAll, the reference contract empties the contract balance (address(c).balance == 0) afterward; the mutant that removes the internal withdraw call can leave a nonzero contract balance, so there exists an input (a positive deposit) for which withdrawAll does not reduce the balance to zero.

For every admissible deposit amount and owner caller, calling withdrawAll on the correct contract empties the contract balance (address(c).balance == 0) after the call; the mutant removed the internal withdraw call so there exist inputs (a positive deposited amount) where withdrawAll does not reduce address(c).balance to zero.

For any non-owner depositor and any positive deposit amount, the contract's owner calling withdrawAll will always reduce the contract balance by at least the deposited amount (i.e., the owner's withdrawAll drains funds originating from other addresses); the mutant that removes the internal withdraw call fails to transfer those funds for some admissible deposit and thus violates this rule.

For any nonzero value deposited into C (via its fallback) by a depositor and then when the owner calls withdrawAll, the correct contract transfers out the entire contract balance (making address(c).balance == 0); the mutant removing the internal withdraw call can leave a nonzero contract balance for some deposit, violating this rule.
After the owner withdraws the contract balance, the caller's (tester) address balance increases by exactly the withdrawn amount (i.e. withdraw always succeeds and transfers full value to msg.sender).

property_summary: Calls to withdraw(...) by the owner never revert (i.e., withdraw should always succeed for any uint value).
The test asserts that calling c.withdraw(value) does not revert (reverted == false).
The owner of C can call withdraw(value) without the call reverting (reverted == false).
An invocation of c.withdraw(value) by the contract owner should not revert (reverted == false).

For any recipient that deliberately reverts when receiving funds, the reference contract C's sendMoney call DOES NOT revert (it ignores the callee's failure), whereas the mutant that uses call-and-require will revert when the callee fails; thus the reference always returns (call succeeds from caller perspective) while the mutant can revert for some inputs.

For any target address and any amount within the contract balance, C.sendMoney(target, amount) never reverts even if the callee reverts on receipt (C ignores the callee failure); the mutant that uses call + require will sometimes revert when the callee reverts, breaking this rule.

For any target contract and amount, C.sendMoney(target, amount) never reverts (it ignores callee failure); the mutant that uses call+require may revert when the callee's receive/fallback fails, so the mutant violates this by making sendMoney revert for some adversarial callee and amounts.

For any adversarial callee that sometimes consumes all gas (i.e. runs out of gas) when called, the reference C's sendMoney never reverts (it ignores callee failures), whereas the mutant that uses call + require can revert when the callee's fallback runs out of gas; thus the property is that sendMoney never reverts for any target and amount, but the mutant will revert for some target/amount when the callee exhausts gas.

Reference C's withdraw(...) sends ETH to owner using transfer which always reverts on failure and forwards 2300 gas, so after calling sendMoney to a reentrant/consuming callee the contract's balance remains unchanged (no unauthorized extra withdrawals happen); the mutant replacing transfer with call{value:...}(...)/require(ok) can be re-entered by a malicious recipient during sendMoney/withdraw sequences and thus can change c.balance/withdraw behavior for some inputs, violating the invariance that c.balance never decreases unexpectedly after a sendMoney call by the owner sequence.

Only the original externally-sending caller (msg.sender) can cause the contract to transfer out ether via withdraw; specifically, after funding C by this contract, calling withdrawAll from this contract always reduces C's balance to zero.
